warmup.q: A Quarkus 3.40 endpoint returns Uni<Payment> and builds it with Uni.createFrom().item(repository.findById(id)), where findById is a JDBC call. Which thread runs that JDBC call?
options: A worker thread, because Quarkus sees the JDBC call
A Vert.x event loop (IO thread), because the method returns Uni
A virtual thread, because Quarkus 3.40 runs everything on virtual threads
The Mutiny scheduler, because Uni is lazy
warmup.why: Quarkus REST picks the thread from the signature: Uni, Multi, CompletionStage, Publisher and Kotlin suspend mean "non-blocking", so the method runs on the IO thread. findById is evaluated while the method builds the Uni, so the JDBC call blocks an event loop. Quarkus can't see inside your method; add @Blocking or return a plain value.

sections.h: In Quarkus REST, the return type picks the thread
sections.html:
Every HTTP request to a Quarkus service is read on a Vert.x event loop, which Quarkus calls an IO thread. The Quarkus reactive architecture guide describes what happens next: the extension that dispatches the request decides whether to call your code right there on the IO thread, which avoids a thread switch, or on a worker thread, a thread from a normal bounded pool. For Quarkus REST (formerly RESTEasy Reactive) the decision comes from your method's signature. Everything in this lesson is pinned to Quarkus 3.40.

A method that returns Uni, Multi, CompletionStage or a Reactive Streams Publisher, or a Kotlin suspend function, counts as non-blocking and runs on the IO thread. Anything else, such as a method that returns a Balance directly, runs on a worker thread.

Java
@Path("/balances")
public class BalanceResource {
    @Inject LedgerRepository ledger;              // JDBC, blocking
    @Inject ReactiveLedger reactiveLedger;        // reactive SQL client, returns Uni

    @GET @Path("/{account}")
    public Balance balance(@PathParam("account") String account) {   // plain value: worker thread
        return ledger.find(account);
    }

    @GET @Path("/{account}/live")
    public Uni<Balance> live(@PathParam("account") String account) { // Uni: IO thread
        return reactiveLedger.find(account);
    }
}
Kotlin
@Path("/balances")
class BalanceResource(
    private val ledger: LedgerRepository,          // JDBC, blocking
    private val reactiveLedger: ReactiveLedger,    // reactive SQL client, returns Uni
) {
    @GET @Path("/{account}")
    fun balance(@PathParam("account") account: String): Balance =      // plain value: worker thread
        ledger.find(account)

    @GET @Path("/{account}/live")
    suspend fun live(@PathParam("account") account: String): Balance = // suspend: IO thread
        reactiveLedger.find(account).awaitSuspending()
}

Read the rule as a promise you make. A Uni return type tells Quarkus "this method won't block", so Quarkus skips the hop to a worker and saves its cost. Break the promise with a JDBC call inside and you are back in lesson 5: every other connection on that event loop waits.

The worker pool is a bounded pool like the ones in the executors track. Quarkus runs blocking endpoints on its own executor, whose size quarkus.thread-pool.max-threads defaults to the larger of 8 × CPUs and 200 in 3.40: 200 threads on a 4-core machine.

try.title: Predict the thread
steps: Without running anything, write down the thread for each Quarkus 3.40 endpoint: (a) public List<Payment> recent(), (b) public Uni<Payment> byId(...), (c) public CompletionStage<Receipt> refund(...), (d) Kotlin suspend fun capture(id: String): Receipt, (e) public Multi<Payment> stream().
Open the lab test DispatcherTest and find the test that encodes the same rules. Check your answers against it.
try.expect: (a) runs on a worker thread; (b), (c), (d) and (e) run on the IO thread. The one people get wrong is (d): a Kotlin suspend function is treated as non-blocking, so a blocking JDBC call inside it blocks an event loop, exactly like one inside a Uni method.

refs.title: Quarkus REST guide at 3.40.1: execution model, blocking, non-blocking

sections.html:
When the signature guesses wrong, you annotate. @Blocking (from io.smallrye.common.annotation) sends a method to a worker even if it returns Uni. @NonBlocking keeps a method on the IO thread even if it returns a plain value. Both work on a method, on a class, or on your jakarta.ws.rs.core.Application subclass to change the default for the whole application. Filters follow their endpoint: under @Blocking they run on the worker, otherwise on the IO thread.

Java
@Blocking                                          // returns Uni, but the body blocks: use a worker
@GET @Path("/{account}/legacy")
public Uni<Balance> legacy(@PathParam("account") String account) {
    return Uni.createFrom().item(ledger.find(account));   // the JDBC call runs right here
}
Kotlin
@Blocking                                          // returns Uni, but the body blocks: use a worker
@GET @Path("/{account}/legacy")
fun legacy(@PathParam("account") account: String): Uni<Balance> =
    Uni.createFrom().item(ledger.find(account))    // the JDBC call runs right here

@Transactional is where the Quarkus documentation disagrees with itself. The Quarkus REST guide tagged 3.40.1 says a method or class annotated with jakarta.transaction.Transactional "will also be treated as a blocking method", because JTA is a blocking technology, and that an explicit @Blocking or @NonBlocking overrides this. The same guide on Quarkus's main branch says the opposite: since 3.35, @Transactional no longer makes a method blocking, the return type decides, and a Uni method that uses JTA needs an explicit @Blocking. The research for this track could not find the code that settles which is right for 3.40.

So don't depend on either reading. Put @Blocking on every endpoint that uses JTA and doesn't return a plain value. It costs nothing when the rule already applies and saves you when it doesn't. When it doesn't, the failure is loud. Before it starts a transaction, Narayana's interceptor in 3.40.1 checks whether blocking is allowed and, on an IO thread, throws BlockingOperationNotAllowedException: "@Transactional cannot start a JTA transaction within a reactive pipeline. If the annotated method is intended to be blocking, ensure it is executed on a worker thread, for example by annotating it with @Blocking. ..."

try.title: Read the rules both ways
steps: Take @Transactional public Uni<Void> post(Payment p). Where does it run under the 3.40.1 docs? Under the main-branch docs? What happens to the JTA interceptor in each case?
Now @Transactional @NonBlocking public Uni<Void> post(Payment p). Where does it run, and what happens?
Check the first answer against the lab test that mentions @Transactional.
try.expect: Under the 3.40.1 docs the first method runs on a worker and the transaction starts normally. Under the main-branch rule it runs on the IO thread, and the interceptor throws BlockingOperationNotAllowedException before your code runs. The second method runs on the IO thread under both readings, because an explicit annotation wins, so it always throws. In every case @Blocking would have given the same, working result, which is why it belongs on the method.

sections.h: What happens when you block an IO thread in Quarkus
sections.html:
Quarkus configures its Vert.x instance differently from plain Vert.x, and the differences change what your logs show.

Setting Plain Vert.x 5 Quarkus 3.40
event loops 2 × CPUs CPUs, at least 2, at most one per 10 MB of max heap
warn about a blocked loop after 2 s 2 s (quarkus.vertx.max-event-loop-execute-time)
include the stack trace after 5 s 2 s (quarkus.vertx.warning-exception-time)
threads for blocking work worker pool: 20 executor: quarkus.thread-pool.max-threads, max(8 × CPUs, 200)

A comment in Quarkus's source explains the event-loop default: twice the number of cores used to be the recommendation, but matching cores 1:1 seemed more reasonable and saves memory. On a 4-core laptop that means 4 event loops instead of 8, so one blocked loop stalls a quarter of your connections.

The stack-trace setting is the friendly difference. This section's demo builds a plain Vert.x instance with Quarkus's settings and blocks an event loop for 3 seconds. The first warning already carries the stack:

plain Vert.x default event loops: 8, Quarkus 3.40 default: max(2, min(3420 MB / 10, 4 cpus)) = 4
[vertx-blocked-thread-checker] WARN io.vertx.core.impl.BlockedThreadChecker - Thread vert.x-eventloop-thread-0 has been blocked for 2770 ms, time limit is 2000 ms
io.vertx.core.VertxException: Thread blocked
	at java.base/java.lang.Thread.sleep(Thread.java:509)
	at workbench.nio.l06.QuarkusLikeLoopDemo.lambda$main$0(QuarkusLikeLoopDemo.java:30)

In a real Quarkus service the line goes through Quarkus's own logging, so the prefix differs, but the message and the stack are Vert.x's. The first frame below Thread.sleep is your endpoint.

Some Quarkus APIs don't wait for the checker. They test where they run and fail at once with BlockingOperationNotAllowedException, which extends IllegalStateException: the JTA interceptor from the previous section, and reading a request body as a blocking stream, which fails with "Attempting a blocking read on io thread". Go one level down and the test is simple. Quarkus asks its IO-thread detectors whether the current thread is an IO thread, and the Vert.x detector in 3.40.1 returns Context.isOnEventLoopThread(), the same call this lesson's lab uses. A fast exception in a test is a better way to find a blocking call than a slow event loop in production.

try.title: Block an IO thread with Quarkus settings
steps: Open QuarkusLikeLoopDemo.java (or the Kotlin twin). Predict the event-loop count it computes for your machine.
Predict whether the first blocked-thread warning comes with a stack trace. Run it.
Run it again with -Pargs=1500. How many warnings now, and why?

code.title: QuarkusLikeLoopDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.nio.l06; import io.vertx.core.Context; import io.vertx.core.Vertx; import io.vertx.core.VertxOptions; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** * A plain Vert.x instance configured the way Quarkus 3.40 configures its own, then blocked for 3 s. * Arg: sleep ms (default 3000). */ public class QuarkusLikeLoopDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { long sleepMs = args.length > 0 ? Long.parseLong(args[0]) : 3_000; int cpus = Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors(); long maxHeapMb = Runtime.getRuntime().maxMemory() / (1024 * 1024); int quarkusLoops = (int) Math.max(2, Math.min(maxHeapMb / 10, cpus)); // VertxCoreRecorder.calculateDefaultIOThreads System.out.println("plain Vert.x default event loops: " + VertxOptions.DEFAULT_EVENT_LOOP_POOL_SIZE + ", Quarkus 3.40 default: max(2, min(" + maxHeapMb + " MB / 10, " + cpus + " cpus)) = " + quarkusLoops); Vertx vertx = Vertx.vertx(new VertxOptions() .setEventLoopPoolSize(quarkusLoops) .setMaxEventLoopExecuteTime(2).setMaxEventLoopExecuteTimeUnit(TimeUnit.SECONDS) // Quarkus: 2 s, like Vert.x .setWarningExceptionTime(2).setWarningExceptionTimeUnit(TimeUnit.SECONDS)); // Quarkus: 2 s, Vert.x: 5 s vertx.runOnContext(v -> { System.out.println("[endpoint] on " + Thread.currentThread().getName() + ", Context.isOnEventLoopThread()=" + Context.isOnEventLoopThread()); try { Thread.sleep(sleepMs); // a JDBC call inside an endpoint that returns Uni } catch (InterruptedException ignored) { } }); Thread.sleep(sleepMs + 300); vertx.close().toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get(); } }

alt.title: QuarkusLikeLoopDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.nio.l06 import io.vertx.core.Context import io.vertx.core.Vertx import io.vertx.core.VertxOptions import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit /** * A plain Vert.x instance configured the way Quarkus 3.40 configures its own, then blocked for 3 s. * Arg: sleep ms (default 3000). */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val sleepMs = args.getOrNull(0)?.toLong() ?: 3_000L val cpus = Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() val maxHeapMb = Runtime.getRuntime().maxMemory() / (1024 * 1024) val quarkusLoops = maxOf(2L, minOf(maxHeapMb / 10, cpus.toLong())).toInt() // VertxCoreRecorder.calculateDefaultIOThreads println("plain Vert.x default event loops: ${VertxOptions.DEFAULT_EVENT_LOOP_POOL_SIZE}, " + "Quarkus 3.40 default: max(2, min($maxHeapMb MB / 10, $cpus cpus)) = $quarkusLoops") val vertx = Vertx.vertx(VertxOptions() .setEventLoopPoolSize(quarkusLoops) .setMaxEventLoopExecuteTime(2).setMaxEventLoopExecuteTimeUnit(TimeUnit.SECONDS) // Quarkus: 2 s, like Vert.x .setWarningExceptionTime(2).setWarningExceptionTimeUnit(TimeUnit.SECONDS)) // Quarkus: 2 s, Vert.x: 5 s vertx.runOnContext { println("[endpoint] on ${Thread.currentThread().name}, Context.isOnEventLoopThread()=${Context.isOnEventLoopThread()}") Thread.sleep(sleepMs) // a JDBC call inside an endpoint that returns Uni } Thread.sleep(sleepMs + 300) vertx.close().toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get() }

try.expect: With a few gigabytes of max heap the memory cap doesn't bite, so the count equals your CPUs (4 here, against Vert.x's 8). The first warning, between 2 and 3 seconds in, already includes VertxException: Thread blocked and the stack, because the warning-exception time is 2 s. With a 1,500 ms block there is no warning at all: the checker only reports a task that has run longer than 2 seconds, so short blocks stay invisible in the logs.

sections.h: @RunOnVirtualThread: blocking code without the worker-pool cap
sections.html:
@RunOnVirtualThread tells Quarkus to run the method on a new virtual thread, instead of the IO thread or a worker. The code stays blocking-style, but waiting no longer holds a pooled thread: a JDBC call, or uni.await().atMost(...) on a Mutiny Uni, parks the virtual thread, and the JDK wakes it when the result is ready. This section's demo shows what the worker pool's cap costs. 200 requests arrive on one IO context, and each makes a 100 ms blocking call:

worker pool (20 threads)   200 calls x 100 ms -> 1,037 ms on 20 distinct threads
virtual thread per call    200 calls x 100 ms ->   113 ms on 200 distinct threads

The Quarkus virtual threads guide compares the three models in one table, and its cons are the part to remember:

Model Runs on Main cost
plain return value worker thread the pool caps concurrency
Uni and friends IO thread more complex code
@RunOnVirtualThread a new virtual thread pinning, monopolization, inefficient object pooling

Pinning means a virtual thread that can't unmount, so it holds its carrier thread while it waits. On Java 21 to 23 that happens when it blocks inside synchronized. JDK 24 removed that case (JEP 491), but native code can still pin, and the guide notes that pgjdbc drivers before 42.6.0 pin often on 21 to 23. Monopolization means CPU-heavy work that never blocks, so it keeps its carrier: virtual threads are for IO-bound work only. And libraries such as Jackson and Netty pool objects per thread, assuming a few long-lived threads; a new virtual thread per request defeats those pools.

Two more things stay true. Virtual threads don't limit concurrency: 200 virtual threads sharing a 20-connection JDBC pool still queue at the pool, so put a semaphore or the pool's own limit in front of anything fragile. And the request still arrives on an IO thread. @RunOnVirtualThread works by moving your code off it.

try.title: Pool cap versus virtual threads
steps: Open VirtualVsWorkerDemo.java (or the Kotlin twin). Predict both times before running.
Give the worker pool 40 threads: change Vertx.vertx() to Vertx.vertx(new VertxOptions().setWorkerPoolSize(40)). Predict the new worker time, then run.

code.title: VirtualVsWorkerDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.nio.l06; import io.vertx.core.Context; import io.vertx.core.Future; import io.vertx.core.Promise; import io.vertx.core.Vertx; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.Set; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** 200 requests arrive on one IO context; each makes a 100 ms blocking call. Worker pool vs a virtual thread each. */ public class VirtualVsWorkerDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Vertx vertx = Vertx.vertx(); // default worker pool: 20 threads Context server = vertx.getOrCreateContext(); // where the requests arrive Thread.Builder virtualThreads = Thread.ofVirtual().name("vt-", 0); // used only on the server's thread for (boolean virtual : new boolean[] {false, true}) { Set<String> threads = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet(); List<Future<Object>> calls = new ArrayList<>(); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < 200; i++) { Promise<Object> done = Promise.promise(); server.runOnContext(v -> { Runnable blockingCall = () -> { threads.add(Thread.currentThread().getName()); try { Thread.sleep(100); // JDBC, a card-issuer call... } catch (InterruptedException ignored) { } done.complete(); }; if (virtual) virtualThreads.start(blockingCall); // like @RunOnVirtualThread else vertx.executeBlocking(() -> { blockingCall.run(); return null; }, false); // like @Blocking }); calls.add(done.future()); } Future.all(calls).toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS); System.out.printf("%-26s 200 calls x 100 ms -> %,5d ms on %d distinct threads%n", virtual ? "virtual thread per call" : "worker pool (20 threads)", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, threads.size()); } vertx.close().toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get(); } }

alt.title: VirtualVsWorkerDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.nio.l06 import io.vertx.core.Future import io.vertx.core.Promise import io.vertx.core.Vertx import java.util.concurrent.Callable import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit /** 200 requests arrive on one IO context; each makes a 100 ms blocking call. Worker pool vs a virtual thread each. */ fun main() { val vertx = Vertx.vertx() // default worker pool: 20 threads val server = vertx.getOrCreateContext() // where the requests arrive val virtualThreads = Thread.ofVirtual().name("vt-", 0) // used only on the server's thread for (virtual in listOf(false, true)) { val threads = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet<String>() val t0 = System.nanoTime() val calls = List(200) { val done = Promise.promise<Any>() server.runOnContext { val blockingCall = Runnable { threads += Thread.currentThread().name Thread.sleep(100) // JDBC, a card-issuer call... done.complete() } if (virtual) virtualThreads.start(blockingCall) // like @RunOnVirtualThread else vertx.executeBlocking(Callable<Any> { blockingCall.run(); "" }, false) // like @Blocking } done.future() } Future.all(calls).toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS) println("%-26s 200 calls x 100 ms -> %,5d ms on %d distinct threads".format( if (virtual) "virtual thread per call" else "worker pool (20 threads)", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, threads.size)) } vertx.close().toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get() }

try.expect: About 1,000 ms on 20 worker threads (200 calls / 20 threads × 100 ms) and about 110 to 130 ms on 200 virtual threads. With 40 workers it drops to about 500 to 600 ms (534 and 598 ms in my runs): Little's law again, throughput = threads / time per call. The virtual version has no such cap, which is its strength and also why you add your own limit in front of a fragile downstream.

analogy: A Quarkus endpoint's return type is a label on a kitchen order. Orders marked "quick" (Uni, suspend) are handled by the waiter at the pass, the IO thread, who never leaves the floor for long. Orders without the label go to the back kitchen, the worker pool, which has a fixed number of cooks. @RunOnVirtualThread hires a temporary cook for each order, who sits down while the oven works and costs almost nothing while waiting. The analogy breaks at the label: a real waiter would notice a forty-minute stew. Quarkus trusts the label completely, so a slow dish marked "quick" blocks the waiter and every table behind them.
world: A payments service on Quarkus with Oracle, JDBC and JTA is a blocking service, and that is fine: give its endpoints plain return types, put @Blocking on anything @Transactional that returns Uni or is suspend, and size the worker pool and the datasource pool together. Reach for Uni only where the whole call chain is reactive, such as a reactive SQL client or the Vert.x web client calling a card issuer. Kotlin teams need one extra rule: suspend does not mean "off the event loop". A suspend fun that calls a JDBC repository blocks an IO thread. When latency jumps while CPU is idle, search the logs for has been blocked for.
mistake: The common mistake is converting a JDBC endpoint to return Uni "to make it reactive": return Uni.createFrom().item(repository.findById(id));. Quarkus sees Uni, runs the method on the IO thread, and findById blocks the event loop while the Uni is built. Nothing becomes reactive. The service just loses the worker thread that used to protect the event loop. Either keep the plain return type, add @Blocking, or switch the data access to a reactive client so the method really doesn't block.

compare.title: The lab's dispatch rules in Kotlin and Java

java.title: DispatchRules.java
java.html: final class DispatchRules { private static final Set<ReturnKind> NON_BLOCKING_RETURNS = EnumSet.of( ReturnKind.UNI, ReturnKind.MULTI, ReturnKind.COMPLETION_STAGE, ReturnKind.PUBLISHER, ReturnKind.SUSPEND); static Target target(Endpoint e) { Set<Marker> m = e.markers(); if (m.contains(Marker.RUN_ON_VIRTUAL_THREAD)) return Target.VIRTUAL_THREAD; if (m.contains(Marker.BLOCKING)) return Target.WORKER; if (m.contains(Marker.NON_BLOCKING)) return Target.IO_THREAD; if (m.contains(Marker.TRANSACTIONAL)) return Target.WORKER; return NON_BLOCKING_RETURNS.contains(e.returns()) ? Target.IO_THREAD : Target.WORKER; } }

kotlin.title: DispatchRules.kt
kotlin.html: object DispatchRules { private val nonBlockingReturns = setOf( ReturnKind.UNI, ReturnKind.MULTI, ReturnKind.COMPLETION_STAGE, ReturnKind.PUBLISHER, ReturnKind.SUSPEND) fun target(e: Endpoint): Target = when { Marker.RUN_ON_VIRTUAL_THREAD in e.markers -> Target.VIRTUAL_THREAD Marker.BLOCKING in e.markers -> Target.WORKER Marker.NON_BLOCKING in e.markers -> Target.IO_THREAD Marker.TRANSACTIONAL in e.markers -> Target.WORKER e.returns in nonBlockingReturns -> Target.IO_THREAD else -> Target.WORKER } }

compare.note: Both encode the same first-match-wins rules; Kotlin's when without a subject reads like the figure, Java uses early returns. The language difference that matters is in Quarkus itself: Java has no suspend, so a Java endpoint is non-blocking only through its return type, while a Kotlin suspend fun with a plain return type is non-blocking too and runs on the IO thread. One Kotlin trap from this lesson's lab: Vert.x 5's Future has a member await(), and in Kotlin a member always wins over an extension with the same name, so a test helper fun <T> Future<T>.await() is silently ignored. The lab's test calls its helper awaitResult() for that reason.

worked.title: Pick the thread for four payment endpoints

steps.say: A payment lookup reads Oracle through JDBC. Plain return type, so it runs on a worker. Nothing to add.
steps.code: @GET @Path("/payments/{id}") public Payment byId(@PathParam("id") String id) { // worker thread return payments.findById(id); // JDBC }

alt.html: @GET @Path("/payments/{id}") fun byId(@PathParam("id") id: String): Payment = // worker thread payments.findById(id) // JDBC

steps.say: A capture endpoint uses JTA and returns Uni because a client library wants one. Under the 3.40.1 docs @Transactional alone would send it to a worker; under the main-branch docs it would run on the IO thread and the interceptor would throw. Add @Blocking and both readings agree.
steps.code: @Blocking @Transactional @POST @Path("/payments/{id}/capture") public Uni<Receipt> capture(@PathParam("id") String id) { return Uni.createFrom().item(ledger.capture(id)); // JDBC inside a JTA transaction }

alt.html: @Blocking @Transactional @POST @Path("/payments/{id}/capture") fun capture(@PathParam("id") id: String): Uni<Receipt> = Uni.createFrom().item(ledger.capture(id)) // JDBC inside a JTA transaction

steps.say: A live feed of payment events comes from a reactive client and never blocks. Multi keeps it on the IO thread with no thread switch, which is the case the reactive model is built for.

steps.say: A settlement report calls a slow SOAP service (2 s) that accepts at most 50 concurrent calls, and finance runs it in bursts of hundreds. The worker pool would cap throughput, so use a virtual thread per request, and put the downstream's limit back with a semaphore.
steps.code: private final Semaphore soapSlots = new Semaphore(50); @RunOnVirtualThread @GET @Path("/reports/settlement/{day}") public Report settlement(@PathParam("day") String day) throws InterruptedException { soapSlots.acquire(); // 1. respect the downstream's limit try { return soapClient.settlementFor(day); // 2. blocks: parks the virtual thread } finally { soapSlots.release(); } }

alt.html: private val soapSlots = Semaphore(50) @RunOnVirtualThread @GET @Path("/reports/settlement/{day}") fun settlement(@PathParam("day") day: String): Report { soapSlots.acquire() // 1. respect the downstream's limit try { return soapClient.settlementFor(day) // 2. blocks: parks the virtual thread } finally { soapSlots.release() } }

lab.title: Simulate Quarkus's dispatch on plain Vert.x
steps: Run the tests. All seven fail with NotImplementedError. Read Endpoint.kt for the types.
Write DispatchRules.target with a when that applies the four rules in its KDoc, first match wins. The four rule tests should pass.
Write BlockingGuard.check: throw BlockingNotAllowedException("Attempting $what on an IO thread") when Context.isOnEventLoopThread() is true.

Write Dispatcher.invoke: receive the request with server.runOnContext { ... }, then run the body there (IO thread), through vertx.executeBlocking(callable, false) (worker) or on a new virtual thread, and complete a Promise with the result or the failure.
Run the tests until all seven pass. Then change false to the default and see which test fails, and why.
hints: Marker.BLOCKING in endpoint.markers reads naturally in Kotlin.
val p = Promise.promise<T>(), then p.complete(value) or p.fail(e), and return p.future(). For the worker branch, vertx.executeBlocking(task, false).onComplete(p) passes the result straight on.
Give the Callable an explicit type (val task: Callable<T> = Callable { body() }); Kotlin can fail to infer Vert.x types whose @Nullable annotation lives in vertx-codegen.
Every request goes through the one server context, so an ordered executeBlocking would make the four 300 ms calls queue: that is what the overlap test catches.

drill.title: Write the dispatch rules from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write a function that takes an endpoint's return kind and its annotations and returns IO_THREAD, WORKER or VIRTUAL_THREAD, using Quarkus 3.40's documented rules. Which rule would you add @Blocking for, to stay safe on any 3.x version?

answer.html: object DispatchRules { private val nonBlockingReturns = setOf( ReturnKind.UNI, ReturnKind.MULTI, ReturnKind.COMPLETION_STAGE, ReturnKind.PUBLISHER, ReturnKind.SUSPEND) fun target(e: Endpoint): Target = when { Marker.RUN_ON_VIRTUAL_THREAD in e.markers -> Target.VIRTUAL_THREAD Marker.BLOCKING in e.markers -> Target.WORKER Marker.NON_BLOCKING in e.markers -> Target.IO_THREAD Marker.TRANSACTIONAL in e.markers -> Target.WORKER e.returns in nonBlockingReturns -> Target.IO_THREAD else -> Target.WORKER } } // add @Blocking to @Transactional endpoints that return Uni (or are suspend): // the 3.40.1 and main-branch docs disagree about the TRANSACTIONAL rule.

alt.html: final class DispatchRules { private static final Set<ReturnKind> NON_BLOCKING_RETURNS = EnumSet.of( ReturnKind.UNI, ReturnKind.MULTI, ReturnKind.COMPLETION_STAGE, ReturnKind.PUBLISHER, ReturnKind.SUSPEND); static Target target(Endpoint e) { Set<Marker> m = e.markers(); if (m.contains(Marker.RUN_ON_VIRTUAL_THREAD)) return Target.VIRTUAL_THREAD; if (m.contains(Marker.BLOCKING)) return Target.WORKER; if (m.contains(Marker.NON_BLOCKING)) return Target.IO_THREAD; if (m.contains(Marker.TRANSACTIONAL)) return Target.WORKER; return NON_BLOCKING_RETURNS.contains(e.returns()) ? Target.IO_THREAD : Target.WORKER; } } // add @Blocking to @Transactional endpoints that return Uni: // the 3.40.1 and main-branch docs disagree about the TRANSACTIONAL rule.

recap: Every Quarkus request arrives on an IO thread. Quarkus REST then picks the thread from the signature: Uni, Multi, CompletionStage, Publisher and Kotlin suspend stay on the IO thread; plain return values go to a worker.
@Blocking and @NonBlocking override the signature on a method, a class or the Application.
The 3.40.1 docs say @Transactional makes a method blocking; the main-branch docs say it no longer does. Put @Blocking on JTA endpoints that return Uni either way.
Quarkus 3.40 runs one event loop per CPU (at least 2), warns after 2 s and prints the stack at 2 s. Guarded APIs throw BlockingOperationNotAllowedException on an IO thread.
@RunOnVirtualThread runs blocking code on a new virtual thread: no pool cap, but watch for pinning, CPU-heavy work and per-thread pools, and add your own limit toward fragile downstreams.

explain.prompt: A teammate changed a JDBC endpoint to return Uni "to make it reactive" and latency got worse under load. Explain what Quarkus 3.40 does with that endpoint and what they should do instead.
explain.answer: Quarkus REST decides the thread from the signature. A Uni return type means the method promises not to block, so Quarkus runs it on the IO thread, a Vert.x event loop, without switching to a worker. Wrapping a JDBC call in Uni.createFrom().item(...) evaluates the call while the method runs, so the JDBC call blocks the event loop and every other connection on it waits. Before the change, the plain return type put the call on a worker thread, which protected the event loop. They should either go back to a plain return type, or add @Blocking if they must return Uni, or switch to a reactive database client so the method really doesn't block. If the reason for the change was the worker pool's limit, @RunOnVirtualThread with a limit on database concurrency is another option.

deeper.html:
A few details from the Quarkus 3.40 sources and docs help when you debug thread choices.

Filters follow their endpoint. A @ServerRequestFilter runs on the worker for a @Blocking endpoint and on the IO thread otherwise, so a filter that does a blocking lookup (say, an API-key check against a database) blocks the event loop for every non-blocking endpoint. @ServerRequestFilter(nonBlocking = true) forces a filter onto the IO thread, which is only safe if it really never blocks.

To check which thread runs your code, log Thread.currentThread().getName() or assert io.vertx.core.Context.isOnEventLoopThread() in a @QuarkusTest. Event-loop threads are named vert.x-eventloop-thread-N, and Quarkus's worker threads usually have executor-thread in their names.

The Vert.x knobs live under quarkus.vertx.*: event-loops-pool-size, max-event-loop-execute-time, warning-exception-time and max-worker-execute-time (60 s). The old quarkus.vertx.worker-pool-size is deprecated in favor of quarkus.thread-pool.max-threads. Raising the event-loop count rarely helps a service that blocks: it only spreads the damage over more loops. Removing the blocking call is the fix.

Finally, a version note on the @Transactional disagreement: the 3.40.1-tagged guide and the main-branch guide were both read for this track, and the code that applies the rule was not found. If you need certainty for your exact Quarkus version, write a @QuarkusTest that calls a @Transactional endpoint returning Uni and asserts which thread it ran on.
